opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to see it is that we've watched this movie before. Go back to around 2017, 2018. People were training language models on very narrow things: a model trained on Wikipedia, a model trained on a particular translation corpus. And they didn't generalize very well. You'd train on one distribution and it wouldn't transfer much beyond that. Then GPT-1, GPT-2 came along, and the move was to train on this enormously broad scrape of the internet. Once the data was broad enough, you started to see generalization that nobody had specifically trained for. The model could do a little translation, a little arithmetic, a little reasoning, without any of that being the objective.

My view is that RL is going through the same transition now. Early RL was very narrow. You trained a model to play Go, or to play Dota, or on one specific benchmark, and of course it didn't generalize, because you'd given it one task. What we're starting to do now, and what I think the whole field is moving toward, is RL on a very wide range of tasks: math, coding, agentic tasks, tool use, long-horizon things. As that distribution gets broader, I'd expect the same phenomenon. The model stops learning "how to do this particular task" and starts learning something more like "how to approach tasks in general": how to plan, how to check its own work, how to recover from mistakes.

I don't think there's anything magical about pre-training that makes it uniquely able to generalize. What makes it generalize is breadth plus scale. Pre-training happened to be the first place we got both. I don't see a principled reason RL can't get there too, and the early evidence we're seeing internally is consistent with that. Training on more varied environments transfers to environments we never trained on.

Now, I'll be honest. It's an empirical bet, like everything in this field. There could be a wall I'm not seeing. But every time I've bet against "make it broader, make it bigger, and it'll generalize," I've been wrong, and every time I've bet on it, I've been mostly right. So that's my prior.

r001.rationale: The candidate says narrow language-model training transferred poorly, while training on a broad internet scrape produced stronger generalization.

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts that RL trained across a wider range of tasks will increasingly generalize to tasks and environments it has not seen.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that I don't have a proof. It's more of an empirical bet, and the bet is grounded in what we saw happen with pre-training.

If you go back to 2017 or 2018, the thing people were skeptical about was exactly this. You train a model to predict the next token on a bunch of text, and the question was, why would that generalize to anything? Why would predicting the next word teach you to reason about code or translate languages or do arithmetic? And the answer turned out to be that if the task is broad enough and the model is big enough, in order to do the narrow thing well, you have to learn the general thing. You can't predict the next token in a physics textbook without learning something about physics. The compression forces generalization.

So my view with RL is that the same logic applies, just one level up. Early RL on language models was very narrow. You'd train on math problems and get a model that's better at math problems and maybe a little better at adjacent things, and people would say, look, it doesn't transfer. And that's true when the task distribution is narrow. It's the same thing you would have seen if you'd pre-trained a language model only on Wikipedia articles about birds.

But what we're actually doing is steadily broadening the distribution of tasks. Math, code, agentic tasks, long-horizon tasks that involve using tools, tasks that involve being honest or careful or recognizing when you don't know something. And what we see, at least so far, is that as that distribution broadens, the skills the model acquires start to look less like task-specific tricks and more like general competencies. Things like checking your work, decomposing a problem, noticing when a line of attack isn't working and backing off. Those aren't math skills or coding skills. They're just what it takes to be good at hard things.

Now, there are differences, and I want to be fair about them. Pre-training data is in some sense free. It's just out there. RL environments have to be built, the reward signals have to be designed, and if you get the reward wrong you teach the model the wrong thing. So the bottleneck shifts from compute and data to something more like the breadth and quality of the environments. That's a real engineering problem and it's one of the things we spend a lot of time on.

But I don't see a fundamental reason it should be different in kind. The scaling laws we observed in pre-training were really statements about what happens when you push a sufficiently general learner on a sufficiently broad distribution. There's nothing in that story that says the signal has to come from next-token prediction specifically. And the early evidence, the stuff we can see internally, is consistent with the same shape of curve. It would be a surprising coincidence to me if the one place that pattern broke was precisely here.

So I'd put it this way. I've been wrong before about timing, I've been wrong about specifics. But every time I've bet that scaling a general method on a broad distribution would stall out, I've lost that bet. I'm not eager to make it again.

r001.rationale: The response says broad pre-training made models generalize beyond narrow next-token tasks, with examples such as physics, code, translation, and arithmetic; it contrasts this with training only on bird articles.

r002.rationale: The response predicts that as RL tasks broaden across areas like math, code, tool use, and long-horizon tasks, the model will acquire more general competencies.

astra-6.text:
I think the intuition is that pre-training already showed us something surprising: if you train on a sufficiently broad distribution, a relatively simple objective can produce capabilities that go well beyond any particular example in that distribution. Predicting the next word sounds narrow, but doing it well across all these different contexts requires learning a lot about the world.

With reinforcement learning, the question is whether we can get a similarly broad distribution of tasks where the model has to figure things out, take actions, and learn from the results. If you train on one narrow task, I wouldn’t expect that to magically generalize. But as you broaden the tasks, there may be strategies that are useful across many of them: checking your work, breaking a problem into pieces, revising an approach when it fails. Learning those could transfer to tasks you haven’t trained on.

The big uncertainty is how broad that distribution needs to be and how good the feedback has to be. Text gives you an enormous amount of training data almost for free. With reinforcement learning, constructing environments and getting reliable feedback can be much harder. So I’d call this a hypothesis with a plausible mechanism, rather than something that follows automatically from the success of pre-training.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training across a sufficiently broad distribution and many different contexts produces capabilities beyond individual examples, linking that breadth to stronger generalization.

r002.rationale: The response predicts that broader reinforcement-learning task distributions can teach strategies that transfer to tasks the model has not trained on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the reason to expect it is that the tasks themselves increasingly require general capabilities. If you train on a narrow game, you can become very good at that game without learning much that transfers. But if you’re training on writing software, doing research, analyzing evidence—these tasks share a lot of underlying structure. You have to form hypotheses, plan, notice when something isn’t working, and try a different approach.

Pre-training gives us one example of this. Predicting the next word sounds like a fairly narrow objective, but when you do it across a sufficiently broad distribution, the best way to succeed is to learn a lot about the world. The analogous argument for reinforcement learning is that, across a sufficiently broad distribution of problems, the best way to get rewarded is to develop methods that work across problems.

Now, that’s an argument, not a guarantee. You could have rewards that are easy to game, or a task distribution that looks broad but actually rewards a small collection of tricks. The empirical question is whether improvements transfer to genuinely different tasks. That’s what I’d look at, rather than just whether the training reward keeps going up.

r001.rationale: The response says broad pre-training distributions can teach models about the world, but does not identify broadening pre-training data beyond narrow text domains as what enabled stronger generalization.

r002.rationale: It predicts that reinforcement learning across a sufficiently broad distribution of problems will favor methods that transfer across problems.
